notes: Wednesday 25 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Mon 23 – Tue 24 Nov (US/Europe). Economy: Huang rally fades, Nvidia -6%, Anthropic below IPO price; US consumer confidence jumps after midterms; EU caps Chinese hybrid imports; France recession warnings. Tech: Schumer accuses Huang of export-control violations; Huawei guilty of trade-secret theft, cleared of racketeering; NY top court clears platforms over Buffalo shooting; Signal blocks AI agents. Politics: Trump may have made up to $15m on Nvidia; Sarkozy and Carla Bruni to face trial; South Korea island air-raid alert over Russian planes; Spain's snap election over housing. Literature (US): Bob Woodward's memoir Secrets; Hemingway and censorship in Four-Letter Nation; Kylie Cheung's Playing the Victim; Carol Davis on architecture and storytelling. Society: Gaza meningitis epidemic alert; Cuba life expectancy falls; US food banks above pandemic demand; Syria land mine casualties soar.

stories.headline: The Huang rally fades: tech stocks fall again, and Anthropic drops below its IPO price
stories.dek: One day after Nvidia's 31% jump, its stock lost almost 6%. Investors are still nervous about AI.
stories.caveman: On Monday, Nvidia brought back its founder Jensen Huang as CEO, and its stock shot up more than 30%, adding over $900bn in value. On Tuesday, the party ended. Nvidia's stock fell almost 6%. The Nasdaq, a stock index full of tech companies, fell 1.48%, and the wider S&P 500 fell 0.5%. The Dow was just barely up. The AI company Anthropic, which sold shares to the public for the first time last week, fell about 6.5% to $81.90. That is below its $83 IPO price, which means people who bought at the start are now losing money. AI stocks had already dropped a lot in November because of worries about profits and the huge amounts of money being spent on AI. In Asia, though, Tuesday was a big day up: Taiwan's top-50 stock index jumped 9.5% and South Korea's rose 6.5%, catching up with Monday's US rally.
stories.why_it_matters: Many retirement funds hold these big tech companies. When a few AI stocks swing this hard, everyone's savings swing with them.
stories.camps: Optimists say Huang's return removes one of the biggest unknowns for AI, so prices should settle. Skeptics say one man coming back does not fix the deeper worries: lots of debt, huge spending, and no proof yet that AI will earn enough to pay for it all.
stories.image_alt: A trader on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange

terms.explain: A US stock index packed with tech companies, often used to track how tech stocks are doing.
A stock index of 500 large US companies; a common measure of the whole US market.
Initial public offering: the first time a company sells shares to the public.
A quick, strong rise in stock prices.

stories.headline: Americans feel much better about the economy after the midterm elections
stories.dek: A big consumer survey jumped 11.4 points in November. Democrats and independents grew more hopeful; Republicans dipped slightly.
stories.caveman: The Conference Board, a research group, asks Americans every month how they feel about the economy. Its main number jumped to 103.3 in November, up 11.4 points from October. Experts had expected only about 92. People said they still hate high prices, but they also see more jobs around and expect inflation to cool a little. The share of people who said jobs are "plentiful" rose to 30.8%, while the share who said jobs are "hard to get" fell to 18.4%. People now expect prices to rise 5.7% over the next year, which is still high but lower than before. The mood split by party: Democrats and independents became much more optimistic after Democrats won the midterm elections, while Republicans became slightly less optimistic, though they are still the most upbeat group. Inflation has been above the Federal Reserve's 2% goal for about five and a half years, and the Fed is expected to raise interest rates by a quarter point in two weeks.
stories.why_it_matters: When people feel good, they spend more, and spending drives most of the US economy. The holiday shopping season starts this week.
stories.camps: Some see real reasons for hope: more jobs and slightly cooler inflation expectations. Others point out that feelings often follow politics, not the actual economy, and that prices, rents and health costs are still squeezing many families.
stories.image_alt: Shoppers look into freezer cases at a grocery store

terms.explain: A survey measure of how good people feel about the economy and their own money.
When prices rise over time, so the same money buys less.
The US central bank. It raises or lowers interest rates to control inflation and support jobs.
US national elections held halfway through a president's four-year term.

stories.headline: EU will cap tariff-free imports of Chinese hybrid cars from 1 December
stories.dek: The limit lasts 200 days while the EU investigates. Japan, South Korea, Turkey and the UK get quotas too.
stories.caveman: Hybrid cars use both a gas engine and an electric battery. More and more of them are coming into Europe from China. The European Commission, the EU's government, says that from 1 December it will cap how many hybrids can come in without extra taxes. For China, the limit is 350,000 cars in the first year, or about 191,000 over the 200 days the rule lasts. That is about half of the Chinese hybrids expected to arrive in the next 12 months. Other countries get limits too: 310,000 for Japan, 230,000 for Turkey, 105,000 for South Korea and 190,000 for the UK. The rule is temporary under World Trade Organization rules, while the EU investigates whether these imports hurt European carmakers. The EU says imports of Chinese electric cars jumped from 21,000 in 2020 to 438,000 in 2024. Europe also wants to shrink its huge trade gap with China.
stories.why_it_matters: Car factories employ millions of people in Europe. Limits like this can protect those jobs, but they can also make cars more expensive for buyers.
stories.camps: Supporters say cheap Chinese cars, helped by state money, could wipe out Europe's car industry, so a pause is fair. Critics say quotas raise prices, slow the switch to cleaner cars, and could start a trade fight with China.
stories.image_alt: Rows of new cars parked at a port

terms.explain: A fixed limit on how much of something can be brought in.
A tax on goods brought in from another country.
A car that uses both a fuel engine and an electric motor.
When a country buys more from another country than it sells to it.

stories.headline: France flashes recession warnings as businesses wait for the 2027 election
stories.dek: Business activity fell to a six-month low in November, and companies are the gloomiest since 2012.
stories.caveman: A monthly survey of business managers, called the PMI, showed that French business activity fell to a six-month low in November. Factories did worse than service companies. Companies are the most pessimistic about the coming year since late 2012, except for the start of the pandemic, and they have cut jobs for seven months in a row. Many businesses are delaying decisions until after the presidential election in April 2027. Polls suggest the front-runner is far-right candidate Marine Le Pen. France also faces high government borrowing costs, a ratings downgrade and a weak stock market, and hundreds of thousands of people protested in October and November over schools, living costs and housing. An S&P Global economist says the chance of a "technical recession" (two quarters in a row of shrinking) has gone up, after the economy shrank 0.1% in the third quarter. Some things could help, like lower energy costs and progress on the budget.
stories.why_it_matters: France is the eurozone's second-biggest economy. If it slows down, all of Europe feels it, including exporters in Asia.
stories.camps: Some economists blame political uncertainty and say growth could return once the election is over. Others say France's problems run deeper: high debt, weak demand and public services under strain. Voters disagree about whether the answer is more spending or less.
stories.image_alt: Protesters carrying a French flag march past a large stone arch

terms.explain: A period when the economy shrinks and jobs are lost.
Purchasing Managers' Index: a survey of business managers; below 50 means activity is shrinking.
The group of EU countries that use the euro.
The interest a government or company pays when it borrows money.

stories.headline: Schumer accuses Jensen Huang of breaking US export laws by shipping advanced chips to China
stories.dek: "Like selling rocket engines to the Soviets," he said. Huang will face questions in the Senate on 3 December.
stories.caveman: The US has rules, called export controls, that stop companies from selling the most advanced AI chips to China. On Tuesday, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer accused Nvidia's reinstated CEO Jensen Huang of shipping "extremely advanced chips to China" and breaking those laws. He compared it to selling rocket engines to the Soviet Union during the space race, and called it a failure of enforcement by the Trump administration. Nvidia's board brought Huang back on Monday after President Trump said he stepped in and told the company Huang was not a national security risk. Questions remain about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), a tech executive accused of acting for China and moving advanced chips to Beijing through her company, Megaspeed. Senator Chris Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer to lead Senate Democrats, called the return "exhibit A" of corruption. Huang is due to appear before the Senate banking committee on 3 December.
stories.why_it_matters: AI chips are now treated like military technology. Whether the rules are enforced affects the US-China power balance, and Taiwan, where most of these chips are made.
stories.camps: Democrats and some security experts say the White House is putting business and personal ties ahead of national security. Trump and Huang's supporters say he did nothing wrong and that Nvidia is too important to the US economy to lose its leader. Nvidia has not been charged with any crime.
stories.image_alt: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

terms.explain: Government rules that block certain products or technology from being sold to some countries.
A group of US senators that oversees banks, trade and some export rules.
An Asian AI data-center company that the US says may have helped move Nvidia chips to China.
Put back into a job after being removed.

stories.headline: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets in a US trial, but cleared of the biggest charge
stories.dek: A Brooklyn jury convicted the Chinese tech giant on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud. It was acquitted of racketeering.
stories.caveman: Huawei is a huge Chinese company that makes phones and telecom equipment. US prosecutors charged it in 2019, after its top executive Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Canada in 2018. After a two-month trial in a Brooklyn federal court, a jury found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 charges, including conspiring to steal trade secrets from rival companies, bank fraud, and conspiring to break US sanctions. Prosecutors said Huawei spent 20 years lying, cheating and stealing to win, including lying to banks about its business in Iran. But the jury said not guilty to the biggest charge, racketeering, which would have meant Huawei acted like a criminal organization. Huawei said that acquittal proves the claims "lack factual basis". Its lawyer said the company grew through hard work and innovation and will push for the lowest possible sentence. Sentencing is planned for September 2027, and Huawei is expected to appeal.
stories.why_it_matters: This case is part of the bigger tech fight between the US and China over who leads in telecoms, chips and AI.
stories.camps: US officials see the verdict as proof that Huawei broke the law and is a security risk. Huawei and many in China see the case as politics, a way for the US to hold back a strong Chinese competitor. The split verdict gives both sides something to point to.
stories.image_alt: Court sketch of Huawei defence lawyer Brian Heberlig giving closing arguments

terms.explain: Private business information, like designs or methods, that gives a company an edge.
Running a business like a criminal organization; a serious US federal charge.
Penalties one country puts on another, such as bans on trade.
Found not guilty.

stories.headline: New York's top court: Facebook, YouTube and Reddit are not liable for the Buffalo racist shooting
stories.dek: In a 4-3 vote, judges dismissed lawsuits saying the platforms helped radicalize the gunman who killed 10 Black people.
stories.caveman: In May 2022, a white gunman, Payton Gendron, killed 10 Black people and wounded three others at a Tops supermarket in Buffalo, New York. He had absorbed racist conspiracy theories online. He is now serving a life sentence. Survivors and victims' families sued social media companies, saying their platforms were designed to push extreme content and keep users hooked, and that this helped turn him into a killer. On Monday, New York's highest court, the Court of Appeals, ruled 4-3 to throw out the lawsuits against Meta (Facebook and Instagram), Alphabet (Google and YouTube) and Reddit. The majority said the families did not show the shooting was a "natural and foreseeable consequence" of how the platforms were built. Three judges disagreed and said the case should go forward. Claims against other apps and Amazon, which owns Twitch, where he livestreamed the attack, were also dismissed. One family's lawyer said they are looking at their legal options.
stories.why_it_matters: Courts are deciding how much tech companies are responsible for what their designs do to people. The answer shapes what apps are allowed to do to keep us scrolling.
stories.camps: Families and online-safety groups say platforms profit from addictive, extreme content and should pay when it leads to harm. The companies and many free-speech advocates say the blame belongs to the killer, and that making platforms liable could lead them to remove far more speech.
stories.image_alt: People gather at a memorial outside the Tops market in Buffalo in May 2022

terms.explain: Legally responsible, so you can be made to pay for harm.
New York State's highest court (in most states this is called the supreme court).
To push someone toward extreme beliefs, sometimes violent ones.
A judge's written disagreement with the majority ruling.

stories.headline: Signal starts blocking AI assistants from reading your private chats on screen
stories.dek: Built-in AI helpers like Gemini and Siri can "see" your screen. Signal says that is a privacy problem.
stories.caveman: Signal is a messaging app known for privacy. New AI assistants built into phones, like Google's Gemini and Apple's Siri with "onscreen awareness," can read whatever is on your screen, which could include your private Signal messages. Signal says that data could then be stored outside its control. So it will block screenshots in its iPhone app, and on Android it will turn on screen protection when it detects an AI assistant trying to read the screen. Signal Foundation president Meredith Whittaker said app makers lack good tools to stop AI agents and called on Apple, Google and Microsoft to provide them. She admitted the fix does not cover everything, such as content already stored on the phone. Signal also warned that agents like Meta's Muse could get access through permissions users give during setup. United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also moved to limit outside AI agents. One survey found 88.4% of 750 organizations had at least one AI-agent-related security breach in the past year.
stories.why_it_matters: AI agents are being sold as helpers that do tasks for you. To do that, they need to see your stuff, and that clashes with privacy.
stories.camps: Privacy advocates cheer Signal for drawing a line. AI companies argue that agents only work if they can see context, and that users choose to turn them on. Some users may find the blocks annoying when they want help.
stories.image_alt: The Signal app shown on a smartphone screen

terms.explain: An AI program that can take actions for you, like reading screens, clicking or shopping.
A picture of what is on your screen.
Settings that decide what an app is allowed to see or do on your device.
When someone gets into data or systems they should not reach.

stories.headline: Trump may have made up to $15m on Nvidia stock after pushing the board to bring Huang back
stories.dek: "I made the deal," Trump told CNBC. His disclosures suggest he may have owned up to 370,000 Nvidia shares.
stories.caveman: Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993. Its board pushed him out this month after reports that he had three affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. Then President Trump stepped in. "I spoke to them, let me put it that way," he told CNBC on Monday. "And I convinced them ... I made the deal." The board brought Huang back, and Nvidia's stock jumped 31.5% that day, adding about $950bn in value. Trump's financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics suggest he may have owned as many as 370,000 Nvidia shares as of 30 September, which would mean a gain of up to $15m, as first reported by the Financial Times. A BBC review of his disclosures found he bought Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m over two years. The forms give ranges, not exact numbers, so the true amount is not known.
stories.why_it_matters: A president has huge power over companies. When he personally helps a company he also owns shares in, people ask whether he is serving the country or his own wallet.
stories.camps: Critics, mostly Democrats and ethics experts, say this is a clear conflict of interest and want stricter rules on presidents owning stocks. Trump's supporters say he was protecting a key American company and its workers, and that the stock gain is a side effect, not the reason.
stories.image_alt: Jensen Huang with Donald Trump at a summit in Washington DC last month

terms.explain: When a person in power could personally gain from a decision they make in their job.
A form officials must file listing what they own, often in ranges.
The US agency that collects officials' financial forms and gives ethics advice.
The group of people who oversee a company and can hire or fire the CEO.

stories.headline: Former French president Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni will face trial over a recanted witness
stories.dek: Prosecutors say a scheme called "Save Sarko" pushed a key witness to take back his claims about Libyan money.
stories.caveman: Nicolas Sarkozy was president of France from 2007 to 2012. He was convicted of conspiring to fund his 2007 campaign with money from Libya's late dictator Muammar Gaddafi, and became the first former French president to go to jail, though he spent only 20 days behind bars. A ruling on his appeal is expected next Monday. Now he and his wife, Carla Bruni-Sarkozy, a former supermodel and singer, will face a separate trial next year. A businessman, Ziad Takieddine, had said he had proof that Libya gave Sarkozy's campaign about 50 million euros. In 2020 he took back his claims. Investigators decided the retraction was not sincere and looked into an alleged operation nicknamed "Save Sarko." The couple will be tried for criminal conspiracy to commit fraud and benefiting from witness tampering. Both deny wrongdoing. Takieddine died last year.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows that even a former head of state can be put on trial, a key sign that the law applies to everyone.
stories.camps: Supporters of the cases say they prove French courts are independent and treat powerful people like anyone else. Sarkozy and his allies say he is being hounded by judges and that the cases are unfair.
stories.image_alt: Nicolas Sarkozy and Carla Bruni-Sarkozy walk together

terms.explain: Illegally pressuring or bribing a witness to change their story.
Taking back something you said before.
Asking a higher court to change a ruling.
When people plan together to do something illegal.

stories.headline: South Korea tells island residents to take shelter as Russian warplanes approach
stories.dek: An air-raid alert went out on Ulleungdo for three minutes. Seoul summoned Russia's defence attaché to protest.
stories.caveman: Ulleungdo is a small volcanic island of about 8,700 people, 120km off South Korea's east coast. Early Tuesday morning, several Russian military planes entered South Korea's air defence identification zone and flew toward the island. The military said they came "to the point just before violating" its airspace, so it warned residents ahead of time. At 7:52am, phones on the island got an emergency alert. The English part said: "EVACUATION, AIR RAID." TV broadcasts told people to get ready to go to underground shelters. Sirens sounded, and South Korean fighter jets were sent up before the Russian planes left. The alert was lifted at 7:55am. Some residents were scared; one man said an elderly neighbor called to ask if war had started. Others said they did not hear the sirens at all. South Korea's defence ministry summoned Russia's defence attaché to lodge a strong protest.
stories.why_it_matters: Russia and China have been flying military planes closer to their neighbors. These flights test defenses and raise the risk of an accident turning into something worse, in a region close to Taiwan.
stories.camps: Seoul calls the flight a dangerous provocation. Some residents and critics questioned the alert itself, saying an "air raid" message for a few minutes scared older people without telling them what to do.
stories.image_alt: TV news broadcast showing a warning message for the island of Ulleungdo

terms.explain: A wide area around a country where it asks foreign planes to identify themselves; it is bigger than its actual airspace.
The sky directly above a country's land and sea, which it controls.
A military officer who works at an embassy.
When fighter jets are quickly sent up to meet unknown planes.

stories.headline: Spain votes Sunday after a housing crisis; the left's Ada Colau calls for a 'rental revolution'
stories.dek: The eviction of an 87-year-old woman sparked nationwide protests and a snap election. Polls favor the right.
stories.caveman: In September, an 87-year-old woman named Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her Madrid apartment. People were furious, and protests spread across Spain. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialist government proposed new housing laws, but right-wing parties and Catalan nationalists voted them down, so he called a snap election for this Sunday. Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona and candidate of a new left-wing alliance called the Broad Front, told the Guardian: "We want to reform the entire rental sector." She said her support for a Socialist-led government would depend on taking properties from "vulture funds," investors who buy up homes to profit from them. Polls say the conservative People's Party (PP) will win the most seats but not a majority, which could make the far-right Vox party the kingmaker. That would bring the far right into government for the first time since Spain became a democracy after the Franco dictatorship.
stories.why_it_matters: Housing costs are a crisis in many countries, from Spain to Taiwan. Spain shows how anger about rent can reshape a whole election.
stories.camps: The left says the market has failed renters and wants strong controls and public housing. The right says rent controls scare off builders and landlords, which makes the shortage worse, and that the answer is building more homes. Many voters simply want lower rent, whoever delivers it.
stories.image_alt: Ada Colau, leader of Spain's left-wing Broad Front coalition

terms.explain: An election called earlier than planned.
Forcing a tenant to leave their home.
A smaller party whose support decides who gets to govern.
A critical name for investment funds that buy cheap property or debt to make big profits.

stories.headline: Bob Woodward, the Watergate reporter, turns his famous questions on himself in a new memoir
stories.dek: "Secrets: A Reporter's Memoir" came out Tuesday. At 83, he names some anonymous sources and admits stories he got wrong.
stories.caveman: Bob Woodward is the reporter who, with Carl Bernstein, uncovered the Watergate scandal that forced President Richard Nixon to resign in 1974. Since then he has written many inside-look books about presidents. His new book, Secrets: A Reporter's Memoir, came out on Tuesday. In it, he writes about his own life: a broken family (his mother left his father for his father's best friend), lucky chances that shaped his career, and stories he did not get right. He says his book on Bill Clinton's White House missed the bigger story of peace and prosperity: "that's my fault." Before the Iraq War, he buried an official's admission that there was no proof of weapons of mass destruction in the 16th paragraph. "That should have been the lead," he says. He also reveals some anonymous sources, either because they have died or gave permission. And he criticizes Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos for staying silent on Trump's attacks on the press, though he says Bezos has not meddled in the news.
stories.why_it_matters: Woodward is a living legend of American journalism. His regrets are a lesson in how even great reporters can miss the real story.
stories.camps: Admirers praise his honesty about his own mistakes. Some journalists question his choice to reveal sources after they die, because reporters usually promise to protect sources forever. Hot right now: the book is one of the season's big releases, backed by a major NPR interview.
stories.image_alt: Bob Woodward smiles at his home in Washington

terms.explain: A book in which a person tells the story of their own life.
A 1970s scandal over a break-in and cover-up by President Nixon's team; it led to his resignation.
A person who gives a reporter information on the promise their name will not be printed.
The opening of a news story, where the most important fact should go.

stories.headline: How Hemingway fought his publisher, and Boston police, over swear words in 'A Farewell to Arms'
stories.dek: A new history of American profanity, 'Four-Letter Nation,' shows how a 1929 magazine cut his dirty words and Boston banned it anyway.
stories.caveman: Literary Hub ran an excerpt from Four-Letter Nation: The Long, Dirty History of American Profanity by historian Steven H. Jaffe (Simon & Schuster). It tells how, in 1929, Scribner's Magazine began printing Ernest Hemingway's war novel A Farewell to Arms in parts, but cut out his swear words. Hemingway was angry; he wanted "full use of the language." His editor, Maxwell Perkins, got a few words put back for the book version, and Hemingway turned others into phrases like "Go something yourself." Even so, Boston's police chief banned the June issue of the magazine from sale for being "salacious." Boston was famous for banning books it called indecent. Jaffe also notes that Hemingway's first novel, The Sun Also Rises, was almost rejected, yet it went on to sell about a million copies by his death in 1961, and young people started talking like his characters.
stories.why_it_matters: Fights over "bad words" in books are fights over who decides what adults may read. Book bans are a hot topic in the US again today.
stories.camps: Free-speech advocates see Hemingway as a hero who pushed literature toward real speech. Others then, and some parents and officials now, argue that communities have a right to set limits on what is sold or taught, especially to young readers.
stories.image_alt: Illustrated cover art for A Farewell to Arms

terms.explain: Swear words or rude language.
When someone with power blocks or cuts words, books or ideas.
A short piece taken from a longer book.
To publish a book in parts, one issue at a time, in a magazine or newspaper.

stories.headline: Kylie Cheung's new book says abusers and powerful states win by 'playing the victim'
stories.dek: 'Playing the Victim' starts with the Johnny Depp-Amber Heard trial and ends with Israel's war in Gaza.
stories.caveman: In 2022, journalist Kylie Cheung was reporting on sexual assault and domestic violence for Jezebel when the defamation trial between Johnny Depp and Amber Heard was streamed live. She saw Depp's team use a tactic psychologists call DARVO: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender. In her new book, Playing the Victim: How Empires and Abusers Fake Victimhood to Hold Power, and How We Fight Back (North Atlantic Books), she argues the same playbook is used by powerful institutions: anti-abortion lawmakers, the US immigration system and, as her central example, the Israeli state, which she says is committing genocide in Gaza. In a Lit Hub interview with Samaa Khullar, Cheung said she first thought the trial was "frivolous" celebrity news, until she saw a huge wave of misogyny against Heard, whom she calls an obvious survivor. She says many people do not understand how abusers work, and that this makes the tactic powerful.
stories.why_it_matters: The book links personal abuse to big politics, a link many feminist writers are making. It also shows how words like "victim" can be used as weapons.
stories.camps: Supporters say Cheung gives readers a clear tool to see manipulation, from homes to governments. Critics will push back hard: Depp won most of his US defamation case, and Israel and its supporters strongly reject the genocide label, saying it is defending itself after the 7 October 2023 attack. The book is clearly an argument, not a neutral report.
stories.image_alt: Author Kylie Cheung next to the cover of her book Playing the Victim
stories.image_credit: Image: Literary Hub / North Atlantic Books

terms.explain: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender: a pattern abusers use to make themselves look like the victim.
Saying false things that hurt someone's reputation; you can be sued for it.
Hatred of, or prejudice against, women.
Acts meant to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, in whole or in part.

stories.headline: Debut novelist Carol Davis picks seven books about how buildings tell stories
stories.dek: The archivist behind the novel 'Restoration' says a novel is built like a house: frames, passages and windows.
stories.caveman: Carol Davis is a writer and archivist whose first novel, Restoration, is out from Rise Books. In a Lit Hub list, she recalls driving through Marin County, California, in 1976 and seeing Frank Lloyd Wright's Marin County Civic Center rise from the hills "as if a spacecraft had landed." That moment started her love of architecture. She says a novel is like a building: it has a frame (beginning, middle and end), passages that lead you from one place to another, and openings that light up or hide a path. Her picks include Gaston Bachelard's The Poetics of Space, Stewart Brand's How Buildings Learn, The Place of Houses by Charles Moore, Gerald Allen and Donlyn Lyndon, and On Architecture by the critic Ada Louise Huxtable. From Huxtable, she takes a lesson: a beautiful building that does not serve the people inside has failed, and a story must serve the reader too.
stories.why_it_matters: Lists like this help readers find older classics through a new writer's eyes, and show how ideas from one art feed another.
stories.camps: Not a debate story. Fans of "quiet" literary fiction will like the idea that rooms hold memory; others may find architecture-as-metaphor a familiar trick. For new authors, a Lit Hub list is a common way to get noticed.
stories.image_alt: An old architectural floor plan of a large house

terms.explain: An author's first published novel.
A person who collects, organizes and protects historical records.
Describing one thing as if it were another, to show how they are alike.
A famous American architect (1867-1959) known for buildings that blend into nature.

stories.headline: Gaza declares a meningitis epidemic alert as cases jump to eight times normal
stories.dek: 272 cases in October alone. Health groups blame destroyed water systems, crowded shelters and sewage.
stories.caveman: Meningitis is a dangerous swelling of the protective layers around the brain and spinal cord. It is often caused by germs and can kill, especially children. Gaza's health ministry issued an epidemic alert after 272 cases were reported in October, more than eight times the normal 30 to 50 a month. Fifteen Palestinians have died of it this year. The UN's humanitarian office had earlier counted 413 suspected cases between 27 September and 31 October, about 68% of them in Gaza City. Health groups say the main causes are destroyed infrastructure, packed tents and schools used as shelters, and drinking water mixed with sewage, made worse by winter floods and limits on aid. Before the war, 80% of Gaza's water came from an underground source that is now polluted by seawater and wastewater. Pipelines from Israel were cut at the start of the war and have only partly reopened. The ministry blames Israel for blocking spare parts, cleaning supplies and fuel.
stories.why_it_matters: Disease often kills more people after a war than the fighting itself. Clean water and sanitation are the first defense.
stories.camps: Aid groups and Gaza's health ministry say Israeli limits on aid and fuel are driving the outbreak. Israel has said in the past that it allows aid in and blames Hamas for diverting supplies. The health ministry in Gaza is run by the Hamas-led authorities, though UN figures show a similar rise.
stories.image_alt: A woman holds her child at al-Aqsa hospital in Deir al-Balah, Gaza

stories.headline: Cuba's life expectancy falls for the first time since records began in 1950
stories.dek: The WHO chief says life expectancy dropped from 78.8 years to 74.4, and baby deaths more than doubled.
stories.caveman: Cuba is an island nation with a communist government and a long-time US trade embargo. On a visit to Havana, World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said average life expectancy fell from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025, the first drop since records began in 1950. The infant mortality rate more than doubled, from about 4 to 9.9 deaths per 1,000 live births. Maternal deaths also rose. Since January, when Washington threatened sanctions on any country that sends fuel to Cuba, the survival rate for childhood cancer fell from 85% to 65%. The 2025 numbers came before that fuel blockade started. Tedros called the health system "critical" and announced $2m for child vaccines and medical equipment. He linked the crisis to sanctions but also to Cuba's "internal problems," and called its new market reforms "positive."
stories.why_it_matters: Life expectancy is one of the clearest signs of how a country is doing. A drop of more than four years is very large and very fast.
stories.camps: Cuba's government and many on the left blame US sanctions and the fuel blockade. US officials and critics of Havana blame decades of one-party rule and a broken economy. The WHO's view is that both matter.

stories.headline: Some US food banks now see more hungry people than at the height of the pandemic, many of them with jobs
stories.dek: Wages are not keeping up with prices, and pandemic-era aid has ended or been cut.
stories.caveman: Food banks are charities that give free food to people who need it. Greg Silverman runs one in New York, the West Side Campaign Against Hunger. During Covid, he once saw a bus driver stop his bus and run over to ask for food. Now, he says, demand is even higher than during the pandemic, and many people asking for food also have jobs. His group expects to give out as much as 6 million pounds of food this year. Across the US, the Agriculture Department found 13.7% of households, about 18.3 million, did not always have enough food in 2024, higher than every year from 2016 to 2021. Pandemic help like bigger SNAP food benefits, the larger child tax credit and free school meals has ended, and the federal government has also restricted food aid. City Harvest says 1 in 5 New Yorkers now face food insecurity, up from 1 in 8 before the pandemic. "Your work and your wages are just not keeping up," its president said.
stories.why_it_matters: Thanksgiving is this week. Hunger in the richest country on Earth shows how living costs can trap working people.
stories.camps: Food-bank leaders and many Democrats want SNAP and child benefits restored or expanded. Those who backed the cuts say government aid became too costly and that a stronger job market is the better fix. Charities say they cannot fill the gap alone.

stories.headline: Two years after Syria's war, land mines are killing children who return to the fields
stories.dek: Nearly 1,000 children have been killed or hurt by explosives since Assad fell. Syria had the second-most mine casualties in the world in 2025.
stories.caveman: Land mines are bombs hidden in the ground that explode when someone steps near them. During Syria's 13-year civil war, both government forces and rebels laid them, often without maps. Since Bashar al-Assad's government fell in December 2024, many families have been going home to old front-line villages and farms. On Sunday, 11-year-old Alaa was looking after her family's goats near her home in north-west Syria when an explosion killed her and badly hurt her 10-year-old brother. Her father said demining teams had visited and people thought the fields were safe. The UN Mine Action Service says nearly 1,000 children have now been killed or hurt by explosives since Assad's fall, and 2,701 people in total. A report published Tuesday by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines found 1,602 casualties in Syria in 2025, up more than 50%, second only to Myanmar. More than 60% of the casualties recorded by the Halo Trust, a mine-clearing charity, happened during farming or herding. "People are taking risks out of desperation," said the Halo Trust's Syria programme manager.
stories.why_it_matters: Wars do not end when the fighting stops. Explosives left behind keep hurting people, especially children, for years.
stories.camps: Everyone agrees mine clearing is urgent. The debate is over money and speed: aid groups say they need far more funding and time, while families who need to farm to survive cannot wait.
